note: The muscle set from which the entire tetrapod appendicular musculature is derived by subdivision. Diogo et al. (2016) reconstruct five muscles per paired fin in the last common ancestor of extant gnathostomes and six in the LCA of extant bony fishes, against the older textbook account of a simple two-mass (adductor/abductor) fin. Records here carry `layer` (superficialis / profundus) as well as `mass` (dorsal / ventral): those two axes give the four-cell classification — abductor superficialis, abductor profundus, adductor superficialis, adductor profundus — that Mansuit & Herrel (2021) use to compare muscle architecture from bichir to horse. Because these muscles are ancestral to BOTH appendages, `derivatives` is split into `pectoral` and `pelvic`.

muscles.name: Abductor superficialis
muscles.developmental: Ventral (abductor) fin muscle mass. In tetrapods this becomes the flexor mass, following the internal rotation of the paired appendages that turned the ventrolateral abductor musculature toward the body.

consensus.origin: Ventral surface of the girdle, and in plesiomorphic taxa the adjacent body wall.
consensus.insertion: Ventral surface of the fin, extending distally to the fin rays. In sarcopterygians it is partially segmented proximo-distally by tendinous intersections.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the spinal nerves supplying the appendage — the ventral/flexor division.

occurrences.name: Abductor superficialis
occurrences.note: One of five muscles per paired fin in Squalus — the plesiomorphic gnathostome condition.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Squalus acanthias. Origin: Ventral pectoral or pelvic girdle bar. Insertion: Ventral surface of the basal and radial cartilages. Not yet resolved to skeleton.json ids — this is the source's prose, carried here so it is not mistaken for a scored attachment.

occurrences.name: Abductor superficialis
occurrences.note: Present in both appendages of Polypterus. Together with the abductor profundus this is the poorly differentiated superficial/deep ventral mass that characterises plesiomorphic actinopterygian fins.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Teleost condition: origin chiefly or entirely on the lateral cleithrum and the posterolateral side of its anterolateral flange, occasionally from the coracoid or even the radials. Insertion diffuse in generalised fishes, consolidating into tendons on the outer anterior bases of the fin rays in more advanced forms — seldom a tendon to the marginal ray.

occurrences.name: Abductor superficialis
occurrences.note: The intersection position differs from the tetrapod developmental pattern, where intersections form in the region of the joints.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Pectoral fin: from the medial faces of cleithrum, extracleithrum and clavicle ventral to the articular process, by broad aponeurosis onto the lepidotrichial bases.

occurrences.name: Abductor superficialis
occurrences.note: Present in both appendages; the pelvic fin retains the complex sarcopterygian condition while the pectoral fin is secondarily simplified.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Pectoral fin: from the lateral faces of clavicle, cleithrum and scapulocoracoid ventral to the articular process. The ventral mirror of the adductor superficialis, and likewise partitioned by tendinous sheets at the axial joints.

occurrences.name: Abductor superficialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. Origin on the ventral cleithral ridge, which Molnar et al. homologise with the longitudinal ridge carrying this muscle's origin on the cleithrum and clavicle of Neoceratodus and with the pectoralis origin of tetrapodomorph fish, the pectoralis being a derivative of this mass. Insertions on the ventral humeral ridge, confluent here with the entepicondyle, and on the strongly developed ventral postaxial process of the ulna, which Andrews & Westoll (1970a) read as a muscle insertion site and as the serial homologue of the ventral process of the humerus; in Latimeria the corresponding process anchors the tendinous intersection dividing the middle portion from the distal. That ventral process is a sarcopterygian synapomorphy, homologous with the tetrapod entepicondyle and ventral humeral ridge (Ahlberg 1989).

occurrences.name: Abductor superficialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tiktaalik roseae. The ventral humeral ridge is confluent with the entepicondyle and undivided — there is no pectoralis process — so the superficial ventral mass is what gets scored here, rather than a pectoralis. Several processes and rugosities on the ventral aspect of the ulna are interpreted as possible muscle attachments (Shubin et al. 2006) but are not assigned, and a crest runs along the preaxial edge of the radius. One node rootward, at Eotetrapodiformes, the ventral process of the radius appears, which Molnar et al. read as the separation of radial from ulnar and distal fin flexors.

occurrences.note: Not one muscle but the whole developmentally ventral superficial series. Ambystoma developmental data show the superficial ventral layer of girdle, arm and forearm comprises pectoralis, flexor digitorum communis, flexor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris, coracobrachialis, humeroantebrachialis and flexor antebrachii et carpi radialis — of which the last two derive instead from pterygialis cranialis.

homology.notes: Diogo et al. (2016) are the first to propose that the abductor and adductor superficialis are homologous with the superficial muscles running from body wall or girdle all the way to the autopodium in tetrapods. The idea is Gadow's (1882): muscles that originally spanned the whole appendage became proximo-distally partitioned at the joints during the fins-to-limbs transition. The novel part is the developmental and comparative evidence, which Gadow lacked.
homology.openQuestion: Gadow's partitioning scenario contradicts the assumption in some fossil reconstructions (e.g. Bishop 2014 on Ossinodus) that stem-tetrapod muscles ancestrally crossed only one joint. The two readings give different muscle maps for the same bones.
homology.teaching: The best single antidote to the 'fish fins had two muscles' claim in textbooks.

muscles.name: Abductor profundus
muscles.developmental: Deep layer of the ventral (abductor) fin muscle mass.

consensus.origin: Ventral girdle, close to the fin articulation.
consensus.insertion: Ventral surface of the proximal fin skeleton.
consensus.action: Depresses and stabilises the fin base.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the appendicular spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Abductor profundus
occurrences.note: In Polypterus the deep groups contribute most of the fin muscle mass — the reverse of the tetrapod condition.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The deep layer of the ventrolateral (abductor) mass. Winterbottom notes the dorsomedial adductor mass separates into two layers before the abductor mass does, judging from Elops.

occurrences.name: Abductor profundus (+ supinator series)
occurrences.note: In Latimeria the deep ventral mass has given rise to a proximo-distal series of supinators. Supinator 1, the most proximal, connects the girdle to both the first and second fin elements.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Pectoral fin: from the medial endoskeleton ventral to the articular process, onto the deep face of the abductor superficialis. Source of the supinator series in Latimeria.

occurrences.name: Abductor profundus
occurrences.note: A short, parallel-fibred triangular muscle. Diogo et al. describe it as 'strikingly similar' to the salamander supracoracoideus in attachments, fibre orientation and overall configuration — the clearest single fin-to-limb muscle correspondence in the paper.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Pectoral fin: from the scapulocoracoid adjacent and ventral to the articular process, onto the postaxial border of the first axial element.

occurrences.note: The supracoracoideus is the second-most-superficial ventral pectoral muscle developmentally in salamanders, matching the abductor profundus position in fish. Latimeria supinator 1 corresponds to the coracoradialis: both are the most proximal of the deep ventral muscles, running from the girdle along the humerus to the radius.

homology.notes: The abductor profundus → supracoracoideus correspondence rests on shared developmental layer position in salamanders plus close morphological similarity in the dipnoan. The deeper derivatives (supinator/pronator series) are argued by the same topological reasoning applied along the proximo-distal axis.
homology.teaching: Pair the dipnoan abductor profundus with the salamander supracoracoideus side by side — the resemblance carries the argument without needing the phylogeny.

muscles.name: Adductor superficialis
muscles.developmental: Dorsal (adductor / 'levator') fin muscle mass. Becomes the extensor mass in tetrapods.

consensus.origin: Dorsal surface of the girdle and the adjacent body wall.
consensus.insertion: Dorsal surface of the fin, extending distally to the fin rays.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal rami of the appendicular spinal nerves — the dorsal/extensor division.

occurrences.name: Adductor superficialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Dorsomedial mass; the first of the two masses to separate into superficial and deep layers.

occurrences.name: Adductor superficialis
occurrences.note: In Latimeria the dorsal muscles of each fin have clear one-to-one correspondences with the ventral muscles of the same fin — the fin is close to a mirror image about its own plane.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Pectoral fin: from the posteromedial cleithrum between anocleithrum and endoskeleton, by a broad tendon onto the bases of the lepidotrichia, with bundles joining pronators 2-3 onto the preaxial radials.

occurrences.name: Adductor superficialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Pectoral fin: arises from the cleithrum and the scapulocoracoid dorsal to the articular process, inserting by aponeurosis onto the distal radials and the bases of the lepidotrichia. The sheet is divided by tendinous partitions that land on the joints between axial elements — Gadow's proximo-distal partitioning, visible in a living fish.

occurrences.name: Adductor superficialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eusthenopteron foordi. The dorsal process of the sarcopterygian humerus — here the ectepicondyle with the deltoid-supinator ridge — carries the superficial dorsal musculature, and one correlate serves two roles because a tendinous intersection lands on it: insertion of the proximal portion, origin of the middle portion. Molnar et al.'s Level I reconstruction at the last common ancestor of Tetrapodomorpha is of exactly this, three divisions each of the superficial adductor and abductor plus the deep adductor; the individually named tetrapod muscles in this column are the speculative part. In tetrapods the same ridge carries the deltoideus and latissimus dorsi insertions and the origins of the extensor antebrachii et carpi radialis, brachioradialis, extensor digitorum and triceps humeralis.

occurrences.note: The dorsal counterpart of the abductor superficialis argument: superficial dorsal muscles running from girdle to autopodium, partitioned proximo-distally.

homology.notes: Mirror argument to the abductor superficialis, and equally dependent on Gadow's partitioning scenario. The dorsal/ventral distinction is the most durable thing about appendicular muscles: it is confirmed independently by innervation, since dorsal-mass derivatives take the radial and axillary nerves and ventral-mass derivatives the median, ulnar and musculocutaneous.
homology.teaching: Establish the dorsal/ventral mass split at the fish level and every tetrapod limb muscle can be placed within it.

muscles.name: Adductor profundus
muscles.developmental: Deep layer of the dorsal (adductor) fin muscle mass.

consensus.origin: Dorsal girdle near the fin articulation.
consensus.insertion: Dorsal surface of the proximal fin skeleton.
consensus.action: Elevates and stabilises the fin base.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal rami of the appendicular spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Adductor profundus
occurrences.note: With the abductor profundus, contributes most of the paired-fin muscle mass in actinopterygians.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Deep layer of the dorsomedial mass.

occurrences.name: Adductor profundus (+ pronator series)
occurrences.note: Gave rise to a proximo-distal series of pronators. The Eusthenopteron humerus preserves osteological correlates of a muscle corresponding to Latimeria pronator 1 — a rare direct fossil check on a soft-tissue homology.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Pectoral fin: from the medial cleithrum and endoskeleton at the articular process, onto the deep face of the adductor superficialis. In Latimeria this deep layer has given rise to the pronator series along the axis.

occurrences.name: Adductor profundus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Pectoral fin: from the scapulocoracoid dorsal to the articular process onto the dorsal face of the first axial element.

occurrences.name: Adductor profundus
occurrences.note: Eusthenopteron foordi. The deep adductor is the seventh muscle in Molnar et al.'s Level I reconstruction at the last common ancestor of Tetrapodomorpha, but no correlate for it is described in this taxon: the facet that carries it just dorsal to the glenoid in Neoceratodus and Latimeria is not reported here. The deep abductor is not among the seven.

occurrences.name: Adductor profundus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tiktaalik roseae. Faint rugosities above the glenoid and a hollow above the coracoid foramen, observed by Molnar et al. on the MCZ cast of NUFV 112 and 'well placed for the origins of deep dorsal musculature' — the mass, not a named muscle. They homologise the shallow fossa on the lateral scapulocoracoid anterodorsal to the glenoid across the whole transition: it carries this muscle's origin in Neoceratodus and Latimeria and the procoracohumeralis origin in Hynerpeton, Ossinodus and captorhinids. That is the girdle end of the fin-mass-to-limb-muscle argument.

occurrences.note: Present as the deep dorsal series rather than as one muscle: the dorsal counterpart of the abductor profundus argument, partitioned proximo-distally from girdle to zeugopod.

homology.notes: The deep dorsal mass gave rise to the pronator series in sarcopterygian fins, as the deep ventral mass gave rise to the supinators. The Eusthenopteron pronator-1 correlate is the strongest palaeontological support for any correspondence in this file.

muscles.name: Pterygialis cranialis
muscles.developmental: Preaxial (radial/tibial side) muscle derived from the ventral (abductor) fin musculature.
synonyms: coracometapterygialis I and II (Polypterus, sensu Wilhelm et al. 2015)

consensus.insertion: Preaxial margin of the fin skeleton.
consensus.action: Draws the fin anteriorly; controls the leading edge.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the appendicular spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Pterygialis cranialis
occurrences.note: One of the five ancestral gnathostome fin muscles.

occurrences.name: Pterygialis cranialis
occurrences.note: = coracometapterygialis I and II of the Polypterus pectoral fin sensu Wilhelm et al.; present in both appendages per Diogo et al.'s own observations.

occurrences.name: Pterygialis cranialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Pelvic fin: from the ventral face of the lateral process of the pelvis, running along the preaxial border to the preaxial lepidotrichial bases. In the pectoral fin it arises instead from the abductor superficialis itself.

occurrences.name: Pterygialis cranialis
occurrences.note: In the pelvic fin, similar to the salamander ischioflexorius.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Recorded from the PELVIC fin — the dipnoan pectoral fin is secondarily simplified to five muscles and lacks it. From the caudolateral face of the pubic ramus to the distal end of the first preaxial radial.

occurrences.note: The forelimb call rests on a developmental observation: in salamanders the preaxial flexor antebrachii et carpi radialis differentiates from a DIFFERENT primordium than the postaxial flexor antebrachii et carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum communis. That separate primordium is the pterygialis cranialis. Distally the ischioflexorius includes the flexor cruris et tarsi tibialis, the preaxial leg muscle corresponding to the preaxial forearm muscle.

homology.notes: One of the two axial-margin fin muscles (with pterygialis caudalis) that are older than any proximo-distal segmentation. Note the exception this creates: humeroantebrachialis and flexor antebrachii et carpi radialis are developmentally ventral superficial muscles but derive from pterygialis cranialis, not from abductor superficialis like their neighbours.
homology.teaching: Shows that a separate embryonic primordium can override apparent layer membership — a concrete case of developmental evidence beating topological appearance.

muscles.name: Pterygialis caudalis
muscles.developmental: Postaxial (ulnar/fibular side) muscle derived from the dorsal (adductor / 'levator') fin musculature.
synonyms: zonopropterygialis (Polypterus pectoral fin, sensu Wilhelm et al. 2015)

consensus.insertion: Postaxial margin of the fin skeleton.
consensus.action: Draws the fin posteriorly; controls the trailing edge.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal rami of the appendicular spinal nerves.

occurrences.note: Absent. This muscle is the sixth added at the osteichthyan node — the difference between the five-muscle gnathostome fin and the six-muscle bony fish fin.

occurrences.name: Pterygialis caudalis
occurrences.note: = 'zonopropterygialis' of the Polypterus pectoral fin sensu Wilhelm et al.; Diogo et al. find it in both appendages. Its shared presence in Polypterus and Latimeria is what places its origin at the osteichthyan LCA.

occurrences.name: Pterygialis caudalis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Pectoral fin: from the postaxial borders of the first to third axial elements together with pronators and supinators 2-4, inserting on the postaxial border between the adductor and abductor superficialis aponeuroses — a postaxial muscle sitting between the dorsal and ventral sheets.

occurrences.name: Pterygialis caudalis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Recorded from the PELVIC fin. From a midline raphe shared with its contralateral partner to the distal medial edge of the first axial element.

occurrences.note: Both derivatives lie on the postaxial side and develop from the dorsal mass. The extensor cruris et tarsi fibularis is the mirror image — dorsal instead of ventral, fibular instead of tibial — of the flexor cruris et tarsi tibialis, and is probably subsumed into the tenuissimus in Ambystoma.

homology.notes: Diogo et al. note that although pterygialis cranialis is ventrally derived and pterygialis caudalis dorsally derived, in some fishes ventral muscles differentiate postaxially and dorsal muscles preaxially — so the mass assignment is a generalisation, not a rule.
homology.openQuestion: The derivation of the mammalian tenuissimus is contested independently by Diogo & Molnar (2014), who derive it from a dorsal tail-region muscle via the reptilian flexor cruris tarsi dorsalis. The two accounts need reconciling.

muscles.name: Retractor lateralis ventralis pectoralis
muscles.developmental: Primaxial: somitic muscle connecting axial skeleton to the pectoral girdle, as distinct from the abaxial muscles of the fin proper.

consensus.action: Retracts and stabilises the pectoral girdle against the trunk.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the anterior spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Retractor lateralis ventralis pectoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: From a cranial rib to the medial face of the cleithrum — the only muscle connecting axial skeleton to pectoral girdle in the dipnoan, which is the basis for homologising it with the tetrapod serratus anterior and levator scapulae.

occurrences.note: The homology rests on these being the only muscles in either taxon that connect the axial skeleton to the pectoral girdle — i.e. the only primaxial muscles. The retractor lateralis ventralis / serratus anterior correspondence was proposed by earlier authors and is endorsed here.

homology.notes: A useful negative result sits alongside this record. The caudofemoralis of Ambystoma, the levator lateralis of Latimeria and the abductor dorsolateralis of Neoceratodus all originate from axial skeleton or axial muscle, so all three fall in the abaxial/primaxial group — but Diogo et al. explicitly decline to homologise them, because the Latimeria levator lateralis belongs to the dorsal musculature while the tetrapod caudofemoralis belongs to the ventral. Shared axial attachment is not sufficient for homology.
homology.teaching: The clearest case in the fin dataset of authors refusing a homology that topology alone would support.

muscles.name: Arrector ventralis
muscles.developmental: Separates from the abductor-arrector anlage — developmentally the first section of the ventrolateral mass to differentiate (Jessen, in Winterbottom 1973).

consensus.origin: Lateral cleithrum, ventrolateral to the abductor superficialis.
consensus.action: Independent control of the leading-edge ray — the basis of the fine pectoral-fin manoeuvring that ray-finned fishes use for braking, turning and hovering.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the appendicular spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Arrector ventralis
occurrences.note: Winterbottom describes the generalised teleost pectoral fin as a pair of muscles either side of the girdle plus a powerful muscle to the marginal ray — arrector ventralis ventrolaterally, arrector dorsalis dorsomedially. All remaining rays are served by a single undifferentiated sheet.

homology.notes: A ray-finned differentiation with no tetrapod counterpart: it serves a single fin ray, and fin rays have no homologue in the tetrapod autopod. Its interest is as a contrast — teleosts achieved fine appendage control by specialising muscles onto individual rays, tetrapods by subdividing masses along a proximo-distal skeletal axis.
homology.teaching: Two different solutions to the same problem of fine appendage control, from the same ancestral two-mass fin.

muscles.name: Arrector dorsalis
muscles.developmental: Dorsomedial counterpart of the arrector ventralis, from the adductor mass.

consensus.action: Elevates and rotates the leading-edge ray.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal rami of the appendicular spinal nerves.

homology.notes: See the arrector ventralis. Together they are the teleost solution to leading-edge control.
